Kgetlengrivier: Enough is Enough

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Residents of Kgetlengrivier took on the local municipality... and won!

Unique Selling Point:
At Carte Blanche we do many stories about poor service delivery and regularly our presenters are standing in rivers of sewage flowing down streets, but we seldom get a chance to showcase a real success story. The tale of Kgetlengrivier Concerned Citizens vs the local municipality is an opportunity to showcase one such victory. The fed-up residents of Swartruggens and Koster in the North West, decided enough is enough and fought for the right to restore service delivery in their towns...

Summary:
The people of Koster and Swartruggens in North West are rejoicing. They have achieved what no other small community in SA has done. A radical High Court decision has changed their lives from being the victims of Municipal mismanagement to being in charge of their own fate. In December Judge Gura ruled in favour of the Kgetlengriver Concerned Citizens, giving them the power to clean their towns up, and to take service delivery in their own hands.

Service delivery in the Kgatlengrivier area has been all but nonexistent for more than 4 years. Sewage was flowing through people’s yards (see pictured attached) and potholes made it difficult to navigate the litter-strewn roads. Only the lucky had water for a few hours per day. 30litres of sewage per second ran into the river. By 2018 the community had enough. The final straw that broke the camel’s back was when the mayor had the road to her mansion paved, this, while most of the community were struggling just to get basic services. Riots broke out and protesters burnt doen several businesses and properties owned by the then-mayor. The municipality was declared disfunctional and the North West was placed under administration.

The community approached the court and were granted a temporary order to step in and help repair some of the damaged infrastructure. But the local municipality was adamant that it would sort out the problems…. at a cost of some R144 million, Kgetlengrivier Local Municipality embarked on a project to build a new sewage works. But residents say it never worked. Despite the Municipality’s interventions residents became desperate, regularly reaching out to the media with pleas for help. The stench was unbearable and sewage was literally flowing through people’s gardens.




Further information:
In an astonishing judgment in the North West High Court in December last year, the judge ordered the imprisonment of the municipal manager, RJ Mogale, of Kgetlengrivier for 90 days, suspended on condition that raw sewage spilling into the Elands and Koster rivers be cleared up within 10 days. Justice Gura also ordered that residents association Kgetlengrivier Concerned Citizens be allowed to take control of the area’s sewage works, to be paid for by the local and provincial governments.

The local government will now have to pay the residents back their R7.5 million which they spent out of their own pockets to fix ailing infrastructure – plus their court costs.

***

In June 2020 4 community members entered a blocked drain to try and clear it of waste and sewage. They were overcome by the fumes and all 4 sadly died.

But even the tragedy of Oom Connie, Oom Christo and the two workers did not dampen their determination to make things better. In late 2020 the Kgetlengriver Concerned Citizens decided enough is enough and they set out to get an order from the High Court to give them the power to take matters in their own hands. They have the expertise and the will, they say, to turn the towns into a functioning, well-run example for all of South Africa.

Following the High Court ruling in December, today there is an air of optimism in the area as residents work together to fix their broken towns. Under the leadership of Mr Carel van Heerden, a group of townspeople have jumped to action, currently fixing the “new” yet dysfunctional sewage system.

Today the Kgetlengriver Concerned Citizens is fuelled by confidence and pride. They realise they have a long way to go, but they are positive and adamant to make life better for everyone in the area.

Script:


KGETLENGRIVIER SCRIPT

MONTAGE: past Carte Blanche service delivery stories.
Claire: Raw sewage is literally flowing in the streets.
Bongani: It’s murky and yep, it smells.
Derek: There’s litter everywhere.
Mac: The smell is unbelievable.
John: Roads, sewage, electricity - all have been impacted by the rot.
LINK
Stories of shocking service delivery are nothing new on Carte Blanche. As presenters we’ve all had our fair share of standing in raw sewage -- it’s almost like a rite of passage… But this time we’re introducing you to a community who seem to have found a solution to their service delivery woes, but is it that simple?
Willie Jones
This is water which is not supposed to be drinkable but smell the water.

Masa: Smells like it came out of my tap.
VO
This is Willie Jones, a local businessman in Koster, one of three towns that make up the Kgetlengrivier Local Municipality in the North West Province.
Willie Jones
I know the water is purified the way it should be -- we’ve got testing equipment...
VO
Since January, Jones has found himself with a new job: running the waterworks and sewage treatment plant in Koster. In a few short weeks, he and fellow residents have restored them to full functionality.
Willie Jones -- Drinks water
Masa: Bravo!
My challenge is.. I want everyone in the country who runs a sewage plant, to do the same.
VO
This is not an illegal hijacking, either. These residents have a High Court order placing responsibility for water and sanitation directly into their hands. It’s the culmination of a years-long battle which has often turned ugly.
Carel van Heerden
In 2018 was daardie politieke oproer gewees in Koster as gevolg van die feit dat die gemeenskap het net gevoel dat die bestuur [...] nie die nodige dienste lewer in terme van wat die grondwet vir ons gee nie.

SUBTITLES: In 2018 there was political uproar in Koster because the community just felt that the management wasn’t providing essential services in terms of the Constitution.
VO
Carel van Heerden chairs the Kgetlengrivier Concerned Citizens. In 2018, when the town was gripped by violent protests and the community had been without water for days, the Concerned Citizens obtained an urgent Court Order allowing them to take over the municipality’s water services for a limited time.
Carel van Heerden
Dit was die aand sesuur gewees toe pomp ons weer water vir die gemeenskap. En toe het ons daardie waterwerke vir ongeveer so ses weke gehanteer.

SUBTITLES: It was six o’clock in the evening when we pumped water to the community again. And then we handled those water works for about six weeks.
VO
Another intervention in 2019 gave more short-term relief but ultimately years of water cuts and raw sewage running directly into the local river, led the people of Kgetlengrivier to say enough is enough.
Carel van Heerden
Ons het gesien dat die munisipale amptenare nie die kennis het, en ook nie die wil het, om ‘n volhoubare diens aan die gemeenskap te lewer nie.
Dit was chaos gewees in Koster. Niks het gewerk nie.

SUBTITLES: We saw that the municipal officials had neither the knowledge nor the will to provide a sustainable solution to the community.
It was chaos in Koster. Nothing worked.
VO
On the 18th of December, the community obtained yet another urgent interim order - this time from the North West High Court in Mmabatho - says local attorney Andreas Peens.
Andreas Peens
So there was an immediate effect to say stop polluting the rivers and file a report as to how the process can better in ten days.
VO
The Municipality was also given 10 working days to come up with a plan to sustainably restore the town’s water supply; failing which, the residents were authorised to take control.
Andreas Peens
The court said, listen Municipality, you have an obligation to the residents, we are affording you an opportunity to rectify the problems. And they simply failed or they ignored the court order.
VO
The 10 days came and went, and on the 7th of January the Concerned Citizens took over both the waterworks and the wastewater treatment plant in Koster.
LINK
This is the R144 million sewage treatment plant built by the municipality. When the residents took it over in early January, it was at a complete standstill.
Willie Jones
Masa: Willie, Let’s talk about the day that you got here. Would you have been able to do what you just did?

Jissie No! Are you mad? It was awful stench. It was covered in condoms, tampons...
VO
Most of the sewage never even made it into the plant, says Jones: it was rerouted into the Koster river… and straight into the Koster dam -- the town’s drinking water!
George Ndlovu
56:29 56:31 - There was a time when we used to drink mud here.
VO
In Reagile, on the outskirts of Koster -- and around the corner from the sewage treatment plant -- residents like George Ndlovu are no stranger to service delivery failures. But even in these forgotten areas, the last few weeks have brought an unexpected change.
George Ndlovu
52:00 From about a week or two ago the water started running for about three days in a row from the dams up there and now we have clean water, we are very happy.
VO
The December Court Order also ruled that Kgetlengrivier Municipal Manager, Joseph Mogale be sentenced to 90 days’ imprisonment, suspended on condition he meet the 10-day deadline.
Andreas Peens
So basically, we are busy pursuing the contempt of court and the imprisonment of the municipal manager at this stage.
V/O
On the 12th of January the Concerned Citizens went back to court. Together with Government, they agreed that a suitable service provider would be appointed to run the waterworks.
Andreas Peens
We needed to finalise a court order that would not be revisable and not be appealable. And that is why we obtained a court order by way of agreement.
Chantelle Gladwin-Wood
[16:13] The ruling in Kgetleng was really unique, because of the fact that the courts actually empowered the residents to appoint a suitably qualified person organization to take control of government services.
VO
Chantelle Gladwin-Wood is a partner at Schindler’s Attorneys and an expert in municipal law.
Chantelle Gladwin-Wood
[07:33] Our law recognizes that our courts are enabled, empowered rather, to create unique solutions to unique problems. So there is a legal basis for people to be going to court to be asking for these kind of unique and novel legal remedies.

Masa: Are we moving in a direction where the court's going to be supporting residents more than in the past?

I certainly hope that we are, because our government in certain instances, has evinced a clear intention to refuse to comply with the law, and we do need our courts to stand up and protect us.
LINK
This actually tastes good - like good clean drinking water. It’s amazing to see what these residents have been able to achieve in such a short space of time, but does it set a risky precedent for other communities to take matters into their own hands?
VO
It’s not the first time residents have attempted to run their own towns. Around the country, frustrated ratepayers have for years refused to pay for services they are not receiving. But Gladwin-Wood says the law isn’t always on their side.
Chantelle Gladwin-Wood
[12:43] [...] There's a difference in municipal law between taxes which are owed to the state, regardless of whether you get one iota of service delivery in return - and taxes here actually include sewerage and refuse charges - and what we call consumption fees or service charges. Now, these are electricity and water charges.
[15:29] [...] You cannot withhold payments of rates and taxes - that is illegal as a rates boycott. But this does not mean that you have to pay for services that aren't delivered.





Prof Pundy Pillay
I think there's a danger in the long run that will have these pockets of resistance all over the country enforcing the kind of racial dichotomy that we've, you know, we struggling to overcome over this past quarter century.
VO
Professor Pundy Pillay is an expert in policy, finance and governance. He says that while we often blame corruption for service delivery failures, more important is a lack of human resources and capabilities at the local government level.
Prof Pundy Pillay
We moved in this country from a highly centralized apartheid system to a completely decentralized, three- sphere system, not taking into account the resources that would be needed and we've neglected, in my view, the local government sphere.
VO
But Pillay says self-governance by residents is not the answer.
Prof Pundy Pillay
[13:10] [...] I think in the longer term, we need to seriously revisit our constitutional setup [...] [21:09] to enable municipalities to have more and better resources to enable them to manage and avoid this kind of crisis.
VO
The Kgetlengrivier Concerned Citizens say they have no interest in replacing government.
Carel van Heerden
[12:50] Glad nie. Ons is nie in die bestuur van die regering betrokke nie. Ons is die waghond om te kyk dat maatskappye en munisipaliteite hulle werk doen vir die dienste waarvoor ons betaal.

SUBTITLES: Absolutely not. We are not involved in the management of the government. We are the watchdog to see that companies and municipalities do their work to provide the services for which we pay.
VO
And they are paying above the odds, forking out R7.5 million so far, to get the water works up and running again: an amount which the municipality must reimburse within 30 days.
Andreas Peens
So ja.. we've rendered the invoice and we're looking forward to payment.






Chantelle Gladwin-Wood
Litigating against municipalities can be a very expensive and also very daunting task. And it can take many years for you to get your money back.
[35:04] Unfortunately, in most of these cases, people are very happy initially to put their money where their mouth is, so to speak. The problem is that this is not sustainable in a long term basis because it costs millions and millions every month.
VO
So the only really long term solution is for residents and the municipality to create a working relationship.
And here the Kgetlengrivier residents have reason to be optimistic. They’ve got the ear of Mmoloki Cwaile, North West Province’s MEC for Cooperative Governance, Human Settlements and Traditional Affairs.
MEC Mmoloki Cwaile
We have persons at the level of municipalities who are simply failing on project planning and implementation [...] whose audit outcomes suggest that they are not complying to legislation and they are simply taking money away from basic services.
V/O
Cwaile has undertaken to work with the Concerned Citizens to secure delivery of services.
MEC Mmoloki Cwaile
The province is now taking over.
It should take the form of a Public-Private Partnership because we intend to work with the ratepayers who have demonstrated their unshakable commitment to serve the people of Kgetleng Local Municipality.
VO
Everyone agrees that there is still a long road ahead. The roads are still full of potholes and litter, and raw sewage still runs into the river - and through Ndlovu’s yard.
George Ndlovu
55:22 - 55:44 I had to wear gumboots. Then I stood this deep in the shit. Then I scoop it into a wheelbarrow and dump it somewhere else. Every time it took me 3 to 4 hours and as you can see my engine isn’t so good anymore.
VO
The Concerned Citizens’ authority is limited to the water works, so they have no jurisdiction to address these wider failures.
But there’s an undeniable scent of hope in the air, and it’s hard to be cynical in the face of their excitement.
George Ndlovu
57:03
Masa: So things are changing...?

Yes, sisi, it looks like things are changing and that makes us happy.
MEC Mmoloki Cwaile
[03:05] [...] It is the matter of reorientating the attitude of the those who are leading our municipalities to appreciate such a rare opportunity of working with those who are even able to sacrifice their own resources for the purpose of saving the people.
Willie Jones
We will keep going until there is a long-term solution.
Carel van Heerden
Ons as inwoners is nie so hulpeloos nie. Ons moet net gaan kyk, daar is genoeg regsremedies om ons te help om ons dorpe volhoubaar saam met die munisipaliteit te bestuur.

SUBTITLES: We as residents are not so helpless. We must just look, there are enough legal remedies to help us manage our municipalities sustainably together with the municipality.


PROMOS

PROMO 1
With failing services and no hope of a turnaround, Kgetlengrivier Concerned Citizens took the municipality to court and won the right to run their own waterworks. But is this a sustainable precedent for the country?
PROMO 2
A ground-breaking precedent has been set as the North West High Court gives Kgetlengrivier Concerned Citizens the authority to run their own water and sewage plants. What could this mean for other failing municipalities?
PROMO 3
For the first time in a long time, Kgetlengrivier residents have clear water in their taps and functional sewage treatment...thanks to a radical settlement with the municipality. But is this letting government off the hook?

SUBTITLES: In 2018 there was political uproar in Koster because the community just felt that the management wasn’t providing essential services in terms of the Constitution. VO Carel van Heerden chairs the Kgetlengrivier Concerned Citizens. In 2018, when the town was gripped by violent protests and the community had been without water for days, the Concerned Citizens obtained an urgent Court Order allowing them to take over the municipality’s water services for a limited time. Carel van Heerden Dit was die aand sesuur gewees toe pomp ons weer water vir die gemeenskap. En toe het ons daardie waterwerke vir ongeveer so ses weke gehanteer. SUBTITLES: It was six o’clock in the evening when we pumped water to the community again. And then we handled those water works for about six weeks. VO Another intervention in 2019 gave more short-term relief but ultimately years of water cuts and raw sewage running directly into the local river, led the people of Kgetlengrivier to say enough is enough. Carel van Heerden Ons het gesien dat die munisipale amptenare nie die kennis het, en ook nie die wil het, om ‘n volhoubare diens aan die gemeenskap te lewer nie. Dit was chaos gewees in Koster. Niks het gewerk nie. SUBTITLES: We saw that the municipal officials had neither the knowledge nor the will to provide a sustainable solution to the community. It was chaos in Koster. Nothing worked. VO On the 18th of December, the community obtained yet another urgent interim order - this time from the North West High Court in Mmabatho - says local attorney Andreas Peens. Andreas Peens So there was an immediate effect to say stop polluting the rivers and file a report as to how the process can better in ten days. VO The Municipality was also given 10 working days to come up with a plan to sustainably restore the town’s water supply; failing which, the residents were authorised to take control. Andreas Peens The court said, listen Municipality, you have an obligation to the residents, we are affording you an opportunity to rectify the problems. And they simply failed or they ignored the court order. VO The 10 days came and went, and on the 7th of January the Concerned Citizens took over both the waterworks and the wastewater treatment plant in Koster. LINK This is the R144 million sewage treatment plant built by the municipality. When the residents took it over in early January, it was at a complete standstill. Willie Jones Masa: Willie, Let’s talk about the day that you got here. Would you have been able to do what you just did? Jissie No! Are you mad? It was awful stench. It was covered in condoms, tampons... VO Most of the sewage never even made it into the plant, says Jones: it was rerouted into the Koster river… and straight into the Koster dam -- the town’s drinking water! George Ndlovu 56:29 56:31 - There was a time when we used to drink mud here. VO In Reagile, on the outskirts of Koster -- and around the corner from the sewage treatment plant -- residents like George Ndlovu are no stranger to service delivery failures. But even in these forgotten areas, the last few weeks have brought an unexpected change. George Ndlovu 52:00 From about a week or two ago the water started running for about three days in a row from the dams up there and now we have clean water, we are very happy. VO The December Court Order also ruled that Kgetlengrivier Municipal Manager, Joseph Mogale be sentenced to 90 days’ imprisonment, suspended on condition he meet the 10-day deadline. Andreas Peens So basically, we are busy pursuing the contempt of court and the imprisonment of the municipal manager at this stage. V/O On the 12th of January the Concerned Citizens went back to court. Together with Government, they agreed that a suitable service provider would be appointed to run the waterworks. Andreas Peens We needed to finalise a court order that would not be revisable and not be appealable. And that is why we obtained a court order by way of agreement. Chantelle Gladwin-Wood [16:13] The ruling in Kgetleng was really unique, because of the fact that the courts actually empowered the residents to appoint a suitably qualified person organization to take control of government services. VO Chantelle Gladwin-Wood is a partner at Schindler’s Attorneys and an expert in municipal law. Chantelle Gladwin-Wood [07:33] Our law recognizes that our courts are enabled, empowered rather, to create unique solutions to unique problems. So there is a legal basis for people to be going to court to be asking for these kind of unique and novel legal remedies. Masa: Are we moving in a direction where the court's going to be supporting residents more than in the past? I certainly hope that we are, because our government in certain instances, has evinced a clear intention to refuse to comply with the law, and we do need our courts to stand up and protect us. LINK This actually tastes good - like good clean drinking water. It’s amazing to see what these residents have been able to achieve in such a short space of time, but does it set a risky precedent for other communities to take matters into their own hands? VO It’s not the first time residents have attempted to run their own towns. Around the country, frustrated ratepayers have for years refused to pay for services they are not receiving. But Gladwin-Wood says the law isn’t always on their side. Chantelle Gladwin-Wood [12:43] [...] There's a difference in municipal law between taxes which are owed to the state, regardless of whether you get one iota of service delivery in return - and taxes here actually include sewerage and refuse charges - and what we call consumption fees or service charges. Now, these are electricity and water charges. [15:29] [...] You cannot withhold payments of rates and taxes - that is illegal as a rates boycott. But this does not mean that you have to pay for services that aren't delivered. Prof Pundy Pillay I think there's a danger in the long run that will have these pockets of resistance all over the country enforcing the kind of racial dichotomy that we've, you know, we struggling to overcome over this past quarter century. VO Professor Pundy Pillay is an expert in policy, finance and governance. He says that while we often blame corruption for service delivery failures, more important is a lack of human resources and capabilities at the local government level. Prof Pundy Pillay We moved in this country from a highly centralized apartheid system to a completely decentralized, three- sphere system, not taking into account the resources that would be needed and we've neglected, in my view, the local government sphere. VO But Pillay says self-governance by residents is not the answer. Prof Pundy Pillay [13:10] [...] I think in the longer term, we need to seriously revisit our constitutional setup [...] [21:09] to enable municipalities to have more and better resources to enable them to manage and avoid this kind of crisis. VO The Kgetlengrivier Concerned Citizens say they have no interest in replacing government. Carel van Heerden [12:50] Glad nie. Ons is nie in die bestuur van die regering betrokke nie. Ons is die waghond om te kyk dat maatskappye en munisipaliteite hulle werk doen vir die dienste waarvoor ons betaal. SUBTITLES: Absolutely not. We are not involved in the management of the government. We are the watchdog to see that companies and municipalities do their work to provide the services for which we pay. VO And they are paying above the odds, forking out R7.5 million so far, to get the water works up and running again: an amount which the municipality must reimburse within 30 days. Andreas Peens So ja.. we've rendered the invoice and we're looking forward to payment. Chantelle Gladwin-Wood Litigating against municipalities can be a very expensive and also very daunting task. And it can take many years for you to get your money back. [35:04] Unfortunately, in most of these cases, people are very happy initially to put their money where their mouth is, so to speak. The problem is that this is not sustainable in a long term basis because it costs millions and millions every month. VO So the only really long term solution is for residents and the municipality to create a working relationship. And here the Kgetlengrivier residents have reason to be optimistic. They’ve got the ear of Mmoloki Cwaile, North West Province’s MEC for Cooperative Governance, Human Settlements and Traditional Affairs. MEC Mmoloki Cwaile We have persons at the level of municipalities who are simply failing on project planning and implementation [...] whose audit outcomes suggest that they are not complying to legislation and they are simply taking money away from basic services. V/O Cwaile has undertaken to work with the Concerned Citizens to secure delivery of services. MEC Mmoloki Cwaile The province is now taking over. It should take the form of a Public-Private Partnership because we intend to work with the ratepayers who have demonstrated their unshakable commitment to serve the people of Kgetleng Local Municipality. VO Everyone agrees that there is still a long road ahead. The roads are still full of potholes and litter, and raw sewage still runs into the river - and through Ndlovu’s yard. George Ndlovu 55:22 - 55:44 I had to wear gumboots. Then I stood this deep in the shit. Then I scoop it into a wheelbarrow and dump it somewhere else. Every time it took me 3 to 4 hours and as you can see my engine isn’t so good anymore. VO The Concerned Citizens’ authority is limited to the water works, so they have no jurisdiction to address these wider failures. But there’s an undeniable scent of hope in the air, and it’s hard to be cynical in the face of their excitement. George Ndlovu 57:03 Masa: So things are changing...? Yes, sisi, it looks like things are changing and that makes us happy. MEC Mmoloki Cwaile [03:05] [...] It is the matter of reorientating the attitude of the those who are leading our municipalities to appreciate such a rare opportunity of working with those who are even able to sacrifice their own resources for the purpose of saving the people. Willie Jones We will keep going until there is a long-term solution. Carel van Heerden Ons as inwoners is nie so hulpeloos nie. Ons moet net gaan kyk, daar is genoeg regsremedies om ons te help om ons dorpe volhoubaar saam met die munisipaliteit te bestuur. SUBTITLES: We as residents are not so helpless. We must just look, there are enough legal remedies to help us manage our municipalities sustainably together with the municipality. PROMOS PROMO 1 With failing services and no hope of a turnaround, Kgetlengrivier Concerned Citizens took the municipality to court and won the right to run their own waterworks. But is this a sustainable precedent for the country? PROMO 2 A ground-breaking precedent has been set as the North West High Court gives Kgetlengrivier Concerned Citizens the authority to run their own water and sewage plants. What could this mean for other failing municipalities? PROMO 3 For the first time in a long time, Kgetlengrivier residents have clear water in their taps and functional sewage treatment...thanks to a radical settlement with the municipality. But is this letting government off the hook?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Residents of Kgetlengrivier took on the local municipality... and won!
metadata.Unique Selling Point: At Carte Blanche we do many stories about poor service delivery and regularly our presenters are standing in rivers of sewage flowing down streets, but we seldom get a chance to showcase a real success story. The tale of Kgetlengrivier Concerned Citizens vs the local municipality is an opportunity to showcase one such victory. The fed-up residents of Swartruggens and Koster in the North West, decided enough is enough and fought for the right to restore service delivery in their towns...
metadata.Summary: The people of Koster and Swartruggens in North West are rejoicing. They have achieved what no other small community in SA has done. A radical High Court decision has changed their lives from being the victims of Municipal mismanagement to being in charge of their own fate. In December Judge Gura ruled in favour of the Kgetlengriver Concerned Citizens, giving them the power to clean their towns up, and to take service delivery in their own hands. Service delivery in the Kgatlengrivier area has been all but nonexistent for more than 4 years. Sewage was flowing through people’s yards (see pictured attached) and potholes made it difficult to navigate the litter-strewn roads. Only the lucky had water for a few hours per day. 30litres of sewage per second ran into the river. By 2018 the community had enough. The final straw that broke the camel’s back was when the mayor had the road to her mansion paved, this, while most of the community were struggling just to get basic services. Riots broke out and protesters burnt doen several businesses and properties owned by the then-mayor. The municipality was declared disfunctional and the North West was placed under administration. The community approached the court and were granted a temporary order to step in and help repair some of the damaged infrastructure. But the local municipality was adamant that it would sort out the problems…. at a cost of some R144 million, Kgetlengrivier Local Municipality embarked on a project to build a new sewage works. But residents say it never worked. Despite the Municipality’s interventions residents became desperate, regularly reaching out to the media with pleas for help. The stench was unbearable and sewage was literally flowing through people’s gardens.
metadata.Further information: In an astonishing judgment in the North West High Court in December last year, the judge ordered the imprisonment of the municipal manager, RJ Mogale, of Kgetlengrivier for 90 days, suspended on condition that raw sewage spilling into the Elands and Koster rivers be cleared up within 10 days. Justice Gura also ordered that residents association Kgetlengrivier Concerned Citizens be allowed to take control of the area’s sewage works, to be paid for by the local and provincial governments. The local government will now have to pay the residents back their R7.5 million which they spent out of their own pockets to fix ailing infrastructure – plus their court costs. *** In June 2020 4 community members entered a blocked drain to try and clear it of waste and sewage. They were overcome by the fumes and all 4 sadly died. But even the tragedy of Oom Connie, Oom Christo and the two workers did not dampen their determination to make things better. In late 2020 the Kgetlengriver Concerned Citizens decided enough is enough and they set out to get an order from the High Court to give them the power to take matters in their own hands. They have the expertise and the will, they say, to turn the towns into a functioning, well-run example for all of South Africa. Following the High Court ruling in December, today there is an air of optimism in the area as residents work together to fix their broken towns. Under the leadership of Mr Carel van Heerden, a group of townspeople have jumped to action, currently fixing the “new” yet dysfunctional sewage system. Today the Kgetlengriver Concerned Citizens is fuelled by confidence and pride. They realise they have a long way to go, but they are positive and adamant to make life better for everyone in the area.
